answer:
Choose artwork as a contextual bandit action conditioned on user, title, device, and placement. The reward should reflect useful viewing or satisfaction, not just clicks on a misleading image. Restrict the action set to approved artwork and keep exploration within product/safety constraints.

Log context, available actions, chosen artwork, probability of that choice, policy version, and delayed outcomes. Epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, or another stochastic policy can provide coverage; deterministic logs cannot support evaluation of actions that had zero chance of display. Offline IPS weights rewards by target/logging propensity, while doubly robust estimates combine a reward model and propensity correction.

Report variance and effective sample size; clipping weights trades variance for bias. Check propensity correctness and account for repeated users and changing catalogs. Confirm offline improvements with an online experiment using viewing satisfaction and retention guardrails. Separate “which title to recommend” from “which image to show,” or their simultaneous changes will confound the measured artwork effect.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** IPS estimates policy value as $N^{-1}\sum_i r_i\pi(a_i|x_i)/\mu(a_i|x_i)$ where the logging propensity $\mu$ is positive for every action the target policy may choose. High weights increase variance. Effective sample size and coverage checks are essential; a formula cannot identify outcomes for actions never explored in the logs. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.4601)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://netflixtechblog.com/artwork-personalization-c589f074ad76) and [2](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/bandits/).
